passage:
'You're out, Tushar's out, and Vidya...' Chinmay paused, enjoying the silence. 'Vidya can be in. If she brings the ball.'
'Why do you always decide?' Vidya asked.
'Because it's my gang. My rules.'
'Tushar cried yesterday, you know. Behind the cycle stand, with his face in his arms.'
Chinmay shrugged, but his ears went hot. 'So?'
'So nobody here actually likes you. They're just scared of being out.'
'That's not true. Ask anyone.'
Vidya turned to the others. 'Who'd still play with Chinmay if he stopped choosing?' Nobody answered. Someone looked at their shoes.
Chinmay's throat went tight. The power had felt so good a minute ago.
'Fine,' he muttered. 'Everyone plays. Tushar bats first.'
Tushar looked up, unsure. 'Really?'
'Really.'

qa.q: What did Vidya say Tushar did yesterday?
qa.a: He cried behind the cycle stand.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when nobody answered Vidya's question?
qa.a: Shaken and hurt; his throat went tight as he saw that the others followed him out of fear, not liking.

qa.q: What did Chinmay change, and why was it wiser?
qa.a: He let everyone play and gave Tushar first bat; including people builds real friends instead of scared followers.

qa.q: How does Vidya see Chinmay's rules?
qa.a: As unfair bossing that hurts people like Tushar and keeps everyone afraid.

grounding: A boy who enjoys deciding who is in or out sees that his group follows him from fear, and opens the game to everyone.

passage: In Class 5, I ran the lunch table. I'm Harsha, and every day I decided who could sit with us. It felt amazing. When Keerthana wore her old sandals, I said she couldn't sit with us that week. Everyone laughed, because they laughed at whatever I said. Then in March I got chickenpox and missed two weeks. Nobody from my table called. Keerthana was the only one who sent a card, with a drawing of a sunflower. I remember holding it and feeling sick in a new way. They hadn't been my friends; they had just been scared of being left out. When I got back, I told everyone the table was open, and I asked Keerthana to sit next to me. I said sorry about the sandals. She said, 'Okay,' and passed me a samosa.

qa.q: Which illness made Harsha miss two weeks?
qa.a: Chickenpox.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel holding Keerthana's card?
qa.a: Ashamed and sick in a new way, seeing that the table had followed out of fear while the person Harsha shut out was the kind one.

qa.q: What did Harsha do on returning, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Opened the table to everyone, invited Keerthana to sit close and apologised; including others made room for real friendship.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt being kept out over her sandals?
qa.a: Hurt and humiliated, yet she still chose kindness by sending a sunflower card.

grounding: A child who ruled a lunch table by deciding who was in or out learns that fear-based followers are not friends, and includes others.

passage:
Wednesday night
Jomon's diary. Today Kalyani told us all to stop talking to Sajan because he 'acts weird'. I didn't even argue. I just turned my back on him at the bus stop like everyone else, and I felt disgusting the whole ride. Last week I laughed when they hid his water bottle. I only do it because I'm scared they'll kick me out and I'll be alone. But then I'm the kind of person who hides water bottles. Tomorrow I'm going to try one small thing: I'll say hi to Sajan. Just hi. No speech. Then I'll see who's still sitting with me at lunch. And if they keep picking on him, I'm telling Ma'am. If nobody sits with me after that, at least I'll know what that group really was.

qa.q: What did the group hide last week?
qa.a: Sajan's water bottle.

qa.q: Why did Jomon go along with ignoring Sajan?
qa.a: Out of fear of being kicked out and left alone, even though it made Jomon feel disgusting.

qa.q: What small step does Jomon plan?
qa.a: To quietly say hi to Sajan without a speech, see who still sits at lunch, and tell the teacher if the picking-on continues.

qa.q: What might Sajan be going through?
qa.a: He is probably confused and lonely, with people turning their backs on him and hiding his things.

grounding: A child writes about joining in with meanness out of fear of losing the group, and plans one quiet refusal.

passage: In the village school near Jorhat, the girls under the peepal tree had a game: whenever Bhupen walked past in his patched shirt, they sang, 'Here comes the scarecrow.' Urmila always sang too, softer than the others. She hated it. But Minoti, who led the group, had once dropped a girl just for not laughing, and nobody sat with that girl for a month. On Monday Bhupen walked past again. The song started. Urmila kept her mouth shut and looked down at her slate. Minoti noticed. 'What's wrong with you?' 'Nothing. I just don't want to.' Minoti sniffed and turned away. Three girls followed her. But Juri stayed, and quietly slid closer to Urmila on the tree root.

qa.q: What did the group sing when Bhupen walked past?
qa.a: 'Here comes the scarecrow.'

qa.q: Why had Urmila always sung, even though she hated it?
qa.a: She was afraid of being dropped, like the girl nobody sat with for a month.

qa.q: What did Urmila's quiet refusal show her?
qa.a: Who truly stood by her: three girls followed Minoti, but Juri stayed beside her.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel hearing the song every day?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt about his patched shirt, and perhaps relieved to notice one voice go quiet.

grounding: A village girl who went along with mocking out of fear quietly refuses once and sees who still stands by her.

passage: For a whole term Joseph had tried to get into the cricket gang that ruled the ground behind the church school in Kottayam. He bowled their balls back, laughed at their jokes, even carried their bats. They never picked him. One Saturday, sitting on the canal wall, he watched Madhuri and Biju racing paper boats, shouting and splashing. They waved at him every week, and every week he had waved back and walked on to the ground. Today he didn't. He climbed down, folded a boat from a notebook page and lost three races in a row. They laughed till their stomachs hurt. Walking home, Joseph realised he hadn't thought about the cricket gang all afternoon. His chest felt light.

qa.q: What did Madhuri and Biju race?
qa.a: Paper boats.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel walking home?
qa.a: Light and happy, and surprised that he hadn't thought about the cricket gang all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Joseph gain by letting go of the cricket gang?
qa.a: Time and energy for Madhuri and Biju, who had waved at him every week and genuinely enjoyed his company.

qa.q: How might Madhuri and Biju see Joseph finally joining?
qa.a: Pleased; they had waved at him every week, hoping he would come.

grounding: A boy stops chasing a popular group and discovers the joy of two friends who already liked him.

passage: In Stockholm, Ingrid had spent all autumn trying to get invited to Elsa's sleepovers. She copied Elsa's braids and learned every dance video. The invitations never came. On Friday, Tomas and Aya asked her, like every Friday, to play board games at Tomas's flat. This time, instead of checking her phone for Elsa's messages, Ingrid said yes and turned it face down. They played a dragon game until they were crying with laughter, and Tomas's dad brought cinnamon buns. On the tram home, Ingrid noticed her shoulders weren't tight. She didn't feel she had lost anything. She felt she had finally arrived somewhere. She took out the braids and let her hair fall loose.

qa.q: What did Tomas's dad bring?
qa.a: Cinnamon buns.

qa.q: How did Ingrid feel on the tram home, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Her shoulders weren't tight; she felt relaxed and content, as if she had finally arrived somewhere.

qa.q: Why was stopping the chase not a defeat?
qa.a: It freed Ingrid's energy for Tomas and Aya, who actually liked her and had invited her every Friday.

qa.q: How might Tomas see Ingrid turning her phone face down?
qa.a: As a sign she was really with them this time, which probably made Tomas glad 🙂

grounding: A girl in Sweden stops chasing a popular girl's approval and enjoys the friends who already like her.

passage:
'Maria sat with Sanya's lot again today,' Zainab said, dropping her bag. 'She didn't even look at me.'
Ammi turned off the stove. 'Since when?'
'Two weeks. After five years, Ammi. Five!' Zainab's voice cracked. 'I know her secret about the maths test. I could tell everyone.'
'You could. How would you feel after?'
Zainab kicked the chair leg. 'Better. For one minute.'
'And then?'
'...Worse.' She sat down. 'I'm so angry.'
'You're allowed to be. Being dropped like that hurts.' Ammi sat beside her. 'Maybe Maria feels torn too. New friends can be a strong pull.'
'So I just forgive her?'
'No. You keep her secret, guard your heart a little, and leave the door open a crack. The rest is up to her.'

qa.q: How long had Zainab and Maria been friends?
qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she thought of telling Maria's secret?
qa.a: Angry and betrayed, wanting to hurt Maria back, though she knew she would feel worse after.

qa.q: What did Ammi suggest instead of revenge?
qa.a: Keep Maria's secret, guard her heart a little, and leave the door open a crack.

qa.q: Why might Maria be acting this way, according to Ammi?
qa.a: She may feel torn, pulled strongly by new friends, rather than simply not caring.

grounding: A girl dropped by her friend for a clique tells her mother, resists revenge, and leaves the door open while protecting herself.

passage: In Class 6, my best friend Avni joined the girls who ran the back row, and overnight I became invisible. I'm Afreen. The worst day was when one of them held up my comic strip and Avni laughed along with the others. My face burned. That evening I wanted to write something horrible about her on the class chart. I told my cousin Sameena Baji instead, and cried until my nose ran. She said I could be as angry as I liked, but revenge would turn me into someone I didn't like. A month later Avni left a note in my desk: 'Sorry. I didn't know how to stay with them and you.' I wrote back, 'I'm still hurt. But you can sit with me at lunch sometimes.' I kept my new friends too.

qa.q: What did one of the girls hold up?
qa.a: Afreen's comic strip.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel when Avni laughed along?
qa.a: Betrayed and humiliated; Afreen's face burned.

qa.q: What did Afreen choose instead of revenge?
qa.a: Telling Sameena Baji and crying it out, then later answering Avni's note honestly while keeping new friends.

qa.q: What does Avni's note suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt torn and sorry, unsure how to keep both the group and Afreen.

grounding: A child betrayed by a friend who joined a clique talks to a cousin instead of taking revenge, and later leaves the door open.

passage: In Class 4B, Uma Ma'am usually started the day with a joke. Today she didn't. Her eyes were puffy, and twice she looked at her phone and then put it face down. Sahil noticed. When she dropped the pile of notebooks by the door, a few boys snickered. Sahil got up and helped her gather them without saying anything. At recess the others planned to make noise in the next period 'because she won't even notice'. Sahil shook his head. 'She looks really tired. Let's not.' He stayed quiet all through the lesson and put his hand up for an answer when nobody else did. Before home time, Uma Ma'am caught his eye and gave him a small, grateful smile.

qa.q: How many times did Uma Ma'am look at her phone?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What did Sahil feel when he noticed Uma Ma'am's puffy eyes?
qa.a: Concerned and caring; he sensed she was tired and worried, so he wanted to help rather than add to it.

qa.q: What small things did Sahil do that helped?
qa.a: He helped gather the notebooks, talked the others out of making noise, and answered in class.

qa.q: How might Uma Ma'am have felt about Sahil's help?
qa.a: Grateful and less alone on a hard day; she gave him a small smile before home time.

grounding: A boy notices his teacher looks tired and worried, and responds with small acts of kindness in class.

passage:
Monday. Uday Sir, who usually made science fun with his magnet tricks, snapped at the back row and forgot to set homework. Jyoti noticed dark circles under his eyes.
Wednesday. At the gate, Jyoti heard him on the phone: 'I'll come to the hospital straight after school.' His voice was small. In class, when the noise rose, Jyoti whispered to her row, 'Let's be quiet today. I think something's wrong at home for him.' Her row went quiet, then the next one.
Friday. Jyoti handed him a card signed by the whole class: 'Hope your week gets better, Sir.' He read it twice and cleared his throat. 'Thank you. That helps more than you know.' Then he did a magnet trick, a small one.

qa.q: What did Uday Sir usually make science fun with?
qa.a: His magnet tricks.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling after hearing the phone call?
qa.a: Concerned and sympathetic; his small voice made her realise he was worried about something at home.

qa.q: How did Jyoti turn her noticing into kindness?
qa.a: She asked her row to be quiet and later gave him a card signed by the whole class.

qa.q: How did the card affect Uday Sir?
qa.a: He was touched; he read it twice, cleared his throat and said it helped more than they knew.

grounding: Over a week a girl notices her teacher is worried and tired, and leads her class in small kindnesses.

passage:
Tuesday. Mrs Pillai was Lavanya's favourite teacher. So when Harish whispered a joke and Mrs Pillai turned and said, 'Lavanya, outside. I expected better,' Lavanya was too shocked to speak. She stood in the corridor, cheeks burning. She hadn't said a word.
Wednesday. Lavanya didn't put her hand up once. At home she told Amma she was never speaking to Mrs Pillai again. Amma said, 'That's one choice. Or you could tell her.'
Thursday. After class, Lavanya waited by the desk, heart thumping. 'Ma'am, on Tuesday it wasn't me talking. It felt really unfair.' Mrs Pillai looked surprised, then sorry. 'Thank you for telling me, Lavanya. I got that wrong.' Lavanya put her hand up in the very next lesson.

qa.q: What did Mrs Pillai say to Lavanya on Tuesday?
qa.a: 'Lavanya, outside. I expected better.'

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling in the corridor?
qa.a: Shocked and hurt; her cheeks burned because her favourite teacher had blamed her unfairly.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than never speaking to Mrs Pillai again?
qa.a: Politely telling her after class that it wasn't her and that it felt unfair.

qa.q: How did Mrs Pillai respond when Lavanya spoke up?
qa.a: She was surprised, then sorry; she thanked Lavanya and admitted she got it wrong.

grounding: Over three days a girl is shocked when her favourite teacher is unfair, then politely tells her how it felt.

passage: 'Ira, you're sulking because Miss said something unfair? Listen to your Salma Nani. When I was eleven, I adored our Urdu teacher, Begum Sahiba. She wrote poems on the board in beautiful curls. One day she tore up my essay in front of everyone, saying I had copied it from my sister. I hadn't. I wrote it myself, by lamplight, over three nights. I felt as if the ground had cracked. I wanted never to read her poems again. My father said, "Go and tell her, politely." So I did, the next week, with the rough pages in my hand. She read them, and her face changed. She said sorry in front of the class. She was only a person, beta. People get things wrong.'

qa.q: What did young Salma bring to show the teacher?
qa.a: The rough pages of her essay.

qa.q: How did young Salma feel when her essay was torn up?
qa.a: Shocked and deeply hurt, as if the ground had cracked, because she had written it herself.

qa.q: What choice in the story mended things?
qa.a: Politely showing the teacher the rough pages instead of cutting her off forever.

qa.q: How might Begum Sahiba have felt reading the rough pages?
qa.a: Surprised and sorry; her face changed and she apologised in front of the class.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a favourite teacher being unfair, and how politely telling her mended things.

passage: 'Thomas, you think your teacher only sees the clever ones? Let me tell you about myself. I'm Hansa Aunty now, but at ten I was the invisible girl at the back. Our teacher always picked the same three girls to read aloud, to carry the register, to lead prayer. I felt like a chair. I sulked for weeks and stopped doing my homework neatly. Then my mother said, "Ask her for something." So I stayed back and asked Madam to help me with long division. She looked at me properly for the first time. "You're Hansa, aren't you? Come early tomorrow." Maybe she had favourites. Maybe she just hadn't noticed a quiet girl. But after that, she did notice me.'

qa.q: What did young Hansa ask the teacher to help with?
qa.a: Long division.

qa.q: How did young Hansa feel at the back of the class?
qa.a: Invisible and left out, like a chair, while the same three girls were always picked.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things for Hansa?
qa.a: Stopping the sulking and staying back to ask the teacher for help.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen young Hansa before she asked?
qa.a: Perhaps hardly at all; she may simply not have noticed a quiet girl, rather than disliking her.

grounding: An aunt recalls feeling invisible to a teacher with favourites, and how asking for help changed things.

passage: With only one day left before annual day, Nirmala Ma'am handed out the last speaking parts, again to the same four girls who always sat in front. Bidisha, who had practised the narrator's lines for weeks, was put in the chorus at the back. She felt invisible. Rain hammered the hall's tin roof, and the rehearsal kept stopping for leaks. During a break, Bidisha almost went to sulk in the corner. Instead she walked up. 'Ma'am, I know all the narrator's lines. Could I be the understudy? And can you tell me what I need to work on?' Nirmala Ma'am blinked. 'I didn't know you'd learnt them. Say the first part.' Bidisha did, over the rain. Ma'am nodded slowly. 'Understudy. And speak louder. You have a good voice.'

qa.q: Where was Bidisha put for annual day?
qa.a: In the chorus at the back.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when the parts went to the same four girls?
qa.a: Invisible and hurt, after practising the narrator's lines for weeks.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do instead of sulking?
qa.a: She asked to be the understudy and asked what she needed to work on.

qa.q: Why might Nirmala Ma'am have overlooked Bidisha?
qa.a: She didn't know Bidisha had learnt the lines, so it may have been not noticing rather than unfairness.

grounding: A day before annual day a girl who feels overlooked by a teacher speaks up and asks for help instead of sulking.

passage: Aadhya's hands shook whenever Mrs Rao walked in. Mrs Rao never smiled, and once she made Ujjwal redo a whole page for messy handwriting. Now Aadhya had a problem: she had missed Tuesday's lesson on decimals, the test was tomorrow, and the school bus left in eight minutes. Ujjwal said, 'Just copy my notes.' But his notes were a mess. Aadhya walked to the staffroom, knees wobbling. 'Ma'am, I was absent on Tuesday. I don't understand decimals.' Mrs Rao looked at her over her glasses. Then she pulled out a scrap of paper and explained it in four quick lines. 'Come tomorrow before assembly if it's still confusing. Asking is good.' Aadhya ran for the bus, grinning. Mrs Rao had almost smiled.

qa.q: How long was it before the bus left?
qa.a: Eight minutes.

qa.q: What did Aadhya's wobbling knees show?
qa.a: She was scared of Mrs Rao and nervous about asking, even though she needed help.

qa.q: What choice helped Aadhya, and why?
qa.a: Asking Mrs Rao directly despite her fear; the teacher explained quickly and invited more questions.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao see a student who asks for help?
qa.a: As a good sign; she said asking is good and offered more time before assembly.

grounding: Under time pressure a girl afraid of her strict teacher asks for help after class and glimpses her softer side.

passage: At the Hyderabad school, everyone whispered that Reena Ma'am had never once laughed. When she called Sonali to the board to solve the geometry sum, Sonali's hands shook so hard the chalk snapped. Her mind went white. 'Sit,' Ma'am said. Sonali sat, cheeks burning. After the bell she stayed back, heart hammering. 'Ma'am, I knew it at home. At the board I get scared and forget.' Reena Ma'am put down her red pen. 'I used to freeze too, in maths, at your age,' she said. 'My teacher let me whisper the answer to her first.' She paused. 'Try that tomorrow?' Sonali nodded. Walking out, she noticed a tiny clay elephant on the teacher's desk, painted pink.

qa.q: What snapped when Sonali was at the board?
qa.a: The chalk.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling as she stayed back after the bell?
qa.a: Nervous and scared, with her heart hammering, but determined to explain what happened.

qa.q: What did asking after class help Sonali discover?
qa.a: That the strict teacher once froze too and would let her whisper the answer first, a way to learn without fear.

qa.q: How might Reena Ma'am have understood Sonali before she explained?
qa.a: Perhaps as unprepared; hearing about the freezing helped her see it was fear, not laziness.

grounding: A girl whose fear of a strict teacher makes her freeze stays back to explain, and finds the teacher's softer side.

passage: 'Aditi, you said Ma'am stayed back to explain fractions? That reminds your Irfan Chacha of something. In Class 5, I was sure I was hopeless at fractions. Everyone else seemed to understand pizza slices, and I just saw circles. One evening Sharma Sir kept me after school. The other teachers had gone home; the peon was locking doors. He cut a guava into halves, quarters and eighths on his desk and let me eat each piece I got right. By sunset I'd eaten most of the guava and understood it all. I said thank you so many times he laughed. After that I worked twice as hard, not because I was scared of him, but because he believed I could.'

qa.q: What did Sharma Sir cut on his desk?
qa.a: A guava, into halves, quarters and eighths.

qa.q: How did young Irfan feel about fractions before that evening?
qa.a: Discouraged and hopeless, because everyone else seemed to understand and he just saw circles.

qa.q: What choice did young Irfan make after the evening with Sharma Sir, and why?
qa.a: He thanked him warmly and worked twice as hard, because feeling believed in gave him confidence.

qa.q: How might Sharma Sir have felt when Irfan kept saying thank you?
qa.a: Amused and pleased; he laughed, glad his extra time had helped 😊

grounding: An uncle recalls a teacher who stayed late to teach him fractions, and how feeling cared for made him try harder.

passage: The storm knocked out the power just as the last bell rang, and Vijay's father phoned to say he'd be an hour late because the roads were flooded. Aparna Ma'am could have gone to the staffroom. Instead she pulled a bench to the window, where there was still grey light. 'Show me your fraction homework, the one you left blank.' Vijay's ears went hot. 'I don't get it.' 'Then let's get it.' She drew rotis on the back of an old notice, and they folded paper strips into halves and thirds. Thunder rolled. By the time his father's scooter splashed up, Vijay had done five sums alone. 'Thank you, Ma'am,' he said, and meant it with his whole chest. At home he did five more without being told.

qa.q: What did Aparna Ma'am draw on the back of an old notice?
qa.a: Rotis.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when he thanked Aparna Ma'am?
qa.a: Deeply grateful and cared for; he meant it with his whole chest.

qa.q: What did Vijay do after that evening, and what does it show?
qa.a: He did five more sums at home without being told, showing new confidence from feeling supported.

qa.q: Why might Aparna Ma'am have used the wait for fractions?
qa.a: She saw he had left the homework blank and cared enough to help instead of resting in the staffroom.

grounding: During a stormy wait a teacher stays to help a boy with fractions, and he feels cared for, thanks her and tries harder.

passage: In the English period, Yamini read her poem aloud, and her voice wobbled on the word 'butterfly'. The teacher smirked. 'Did everyone hear our little opera singer?' The class laughed. Yamini stared at her desk and wished the floor would open. Hansa, beside her, squeezed her hand under the table. At lunch Yamini couldn't eat. 'That was mean of her,' Hansa said. 'Not your fault. Tell your mum today.' That evening Yamini told Amma everything, her voice small. Amma listened without interrupting, then hugged her. 'A teacher should correct you, never shame you. That was wrong.' Before dinner, Amma wrote to the principal asking for a meeting, and read the message to Yamini before sending it.

qa.q: Which word did Yamini's voice wobble on?
qa.a: 'Butterfly'.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: Humiliated and ashamed; she wished the floor would open and couldn't eat at lunch.

qa.q: What did Amma do that same evening?
qa.a: Listened, said it was wrong and not Yamini's fault, and wrote to the principal asking for a meeting.

qa.q: How did Hansa see what the teacher did?
qa.a: As mean and unfair; Hansa squeezed Yamini's hand and urged Yamini to tell her mum.

grounding: A girl mocked by a teacher in class tells her mother, who says it was wrong and raises it with the school the same evening.

passage:
Monday. In PE, Aditi dropped the ball twice, and Ms Kapoor shouted, 'Look, everyone, butterfingers strikes again!' and made her stand at the side for the rest of the game. Some kids laughed. Aditi wanted to disappear into the ground. At home she said nothing and went to bed early.
Tuesday. Mumma found her crying over her PE shoes. Aditi told her. Mumma's jaw set. 'Being mocked like that is not okay. It's not your fault.' She called the school that same morning.
Wednesday. Mumma and Papa met the counsellor, Mrs Chandrika Rao, and the principal. That afternoon Ms Kapoor took Aditi aside and said sorry. 'I was wrong to embarrass you.' Aditi still felt shaky in PE, but she caught the ball once.

qa.q: What did Ms Kapoor call Aditi?
qa.a: Butterfingers.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling on Monday night?
qa.a: Humiliated and ashamed; she said nothing and went to bed early.

qa.q: What did Aditi's parents do once they knew?
qa.a: Mumma said it wasn't her fault and called the school; the next day the parents met the counsellor and the principal.

qa.q: What might Ms Kapoor have felt when she said sorry?
qa.a: Perhaps embarrassed and regretful after realising she had shamed Aditi.

grounding: Over three days a girl shamed by a teacher in front of the class tells her mother, and her parents raise it with the school.
